{{Short description|Matrix used to analyze the stability of a polynomial by its coefficients}}
{{About|the matrices used to check stability of polynomials|matrices whose eigenvalues have negative real part|Hurwitz-stable matrix}}

In [[mathematics]], the '''Routh–Hurwitz matrix''',<ref>{{cite book |last1=Horn |first1=Roger |last2=Johnson |first2=Charles |title=Topics in matrix analysis |date=1991 |isbn=0-521-30587-X |page=101|publisher=Cambridge University Press }}</ref> or more commonly just '''Hurwitz matrix''', corresponding to a polynomial is a particular matrix whose nonzero entries are coefficients of the polynomial.

==Hurwitz matrix and the Hurwitz stability criterion==
Namely, given a real polynomial
:<math>p(z)=a_{0}z^n+a_{1}z^{n-1}+\cdots+a_{n-1}z+a_n</math>
the <math>n\times n</math> [[square matrix]]
:<math>
H=
\begin{pmatrix}
a_1 & a_3 & a_5 & \dots & \dots & \dots & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
a_0 & a_2 & a_4 & & & & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
0 & a_1 & a_3 & & & & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\
\vdots & a_0 & a_2 & \ddots & & & 0 & \vdots & \vdots \\
\vdots & 0 & a_1 & & \ddots & & a_n & \vdots & \vdots \\
\vdots & \vdots  & a_0 & & & \ddots &  a_{n-1} & 0 & \vdots \\
\vdots & \vdots  & 0 & & & & a_{n-2} & a_n & \vdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & & & a_{n-3} & a_{n-1} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \dots & \dots & \dots & a_{n-4} & a_{n-2} & a_n
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
is called Hurwitz matrix corresponding to the polynomial <math>p</math>. It was established by [[Adolf Hurwitz]] in 1895 that a real polynomial with <math>a_0 > 0</math> is [[Stable polynomial|stable]]
(that is, all its roots have strictly negative real part) if and only if all the leading principal [[Minor (linear algebra)|minors]] of the matrix <math>H(p)</math> are positive:

:<math>
\begin{align}
\Delta_1(p) &= \begin{vmatrix} a_{1} \end{vmatrix} &&=a_{1} > 0 \\[2mm]
\Delta_2(p) &= \begin{vmatrix}
   a_{1} & a_{3} \\
   a_{0} & a_{2} \\
   \end{vmatrix} &&= a_2 a_1 - a_0 a_3 > 0\\[2mm]
\Delta_3(p) &= \begin{vmatrix}
   a_{1} & a_{3} & a_{5} \\
   a_{0} & a_{2} & a_{4} \\
   0     & a_{1} & a_{3} \\
\end{vmatrix} &&= a_3 \Delta_2 - a_1 (a_1 a_4 - a_0 a_5 ) > 0
\end{align}
</math>
and so on. The minors <math>\Delta_k(p)</math> are called the [[Hurwitz determinant]]s. Similarly, if <math>a_0 < 0</math> then the polynomial is stable if and only if the principal minors have alternating signs starting with a negative one.

==Example==

As an example, consider the matrix
:<math>
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
-1 & -1 & 0 \\
1 & -1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & -1 
\end{pmatrix},
</math>
and let
:<math>
\begin{align}
p(x)&=\det(xI-M)\\
&=
\begin{vmatrix}
x+1 & 1 & 0 \\
-1 & x+1 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & x+1 
\end{vmatrix}\\
&=(x+1)^3-(1)(-1)(x+1)\\
&=x^3+3x^2+4x+2
\end{align}
</math>
be the [[characteristic polynomial]] of <math>M</math>. The Routh–Hurwitz matrix{{NoteTag|name=confusion|Both Routh–Hurwitz and Hurwitz-stable matrices are more commonly referred to simply as Hurwitz matrices. To reduce the risk of confusion, this section avoids that terminology.}} associated to <math>p</math> is then
:<math>
H=
\begin{pmatrix}
3 & 2 & 0 \\
1 & 4 & 0 \\
0 & 3 & 2 
\end{pmatrix}.
</math>
The leading principal minors of <math>H</math> are
:<math>
\begin{align}
\Delta_1(p) &= \begin{vmatrix} 3\end{vmatrix} &&=3>0\\[2mm]
\Delta_2(p) &= \begin{vmatrix}
   3 & 2 \\
   1 & 4 \\
   \end{vmatrix} &&= 12 - 2 = 10 > 0\\[2mm]
\Delta_3(p) &= \begin{vmatrix}
   3 & 2 & 0 \\
   1 & 4 & 0 \\
   0 & 3 & 2 \\
\end{vmatrix} &&= 2\Delta_2(p)=20 > 0.
\end{align}
</math>
Since the leading principal minors are all positive, all of the roots of <math>p</math> have negative real part. Moreover, since <math>p</math> is the characteristic polynomial of <math>M</math>, it follows that all the eigenvalues of <math>M</math> have negative real part, and hence <math>M</math> is a [[Hurwitz-stable matrix]].{{NoteTag|name=confusion}}
